## 2. Recommended Neovim setup

Since you already use `[[wikilinks]]`, the best-fitting plugin is **telekasten.nvim** or **obsidian.nvim**. I'd pick **telekasten.nvim** — it's purpose-built for Zettelkasten, uses `[[links]]`, and doesn't force Obsidian conventions.

```lua
-- lazy.nvim spec
{
  "nvim-telekasten/telekasten.nvim",
  dependencies = { "nvim-telescope/telescope.nvim" },
  config = function()
    require("telekasten").setup({
      home = vim.fn.expand("~/www/wiki"),
      -- keep GitHub-wiki style so it renders online too
      extension = ".md",
      -- flat vault (no subdir per note), matches your current layout
      dailies = vim.fn.expand("~/www/wiki/journal"),
      templates = vim.fn.expand("~/www/wiki/templates"),
      new_note_filename = "title",   -- human-readable names, not timestamps
      template_new_note = vim.fn.expand("~/www/wiki/templates/new_note.md"),
    })
    -- handy keymaps
    local map = vim.keymap.set
    map("n", "<leader>zf", "<cmd>Telekasten find_notes<cr>")
    map("n", "<leader>zg", "<cmd>Telekasten search_notes<cr>")  -- full-text
    map("n", "<leader>zd", "<cmd>Telekasten find_daily_notes<cr>")
    map("n", "<leader>zz", "<cmd>Telekasten follow_link<cr>")   -- jump on [[link]]
    map("n", "<leader>zn", "<cmd>Telekasten new_note<cr>")
    map("n", "<leader>zb", "<cmd>Telekasten show_backlinks<cr>") -- who links here
    map("n", "<leader>zt", "<cmd>Telekasten show_tags<cr>")
    map("n", "<leader>zi", "<cmd>Telekasten insert_link<cr>")   -- pick + insert [[link]]
  end,
}
```

The killer features for Zettelkasten: **`follow_link`** (jump through `[[links]]`), **`show_backlinks`** (see what references the current note — this is what makes a Zettelkasten a graph), and **`insert_link`** (fuzzy-pick a note to link, so you never mistype names).

## 3. Workflow / structure conventions

- **Keep it flat.** Real Zettelkasten discourages folders; use `[[links]]` and `#tags` as your structure instead. Your `_Sidebar.md` is already a good "index/hub note". Consider one hub note per topic (`Network.md`, `Learning.md` already do this).
- **Naming:** GitHub Wiki links match by title, so `[[OSI Model]]` needs file `OSI-Model.md` *or* `OSI Model.md`. Pick one convention. Spaces work but hyphens are safer cross-tool. Note: emojis in filenames (`🧠 Lifelong Leaner.md`) can confuse some tools — consider plain filenames with the emoji only in the `# Heading`.
- **Add tags** with `#tag` inline so `show_tags` builds an index for free.
- **Backlinks over hierarchy:** when you write a note, link generously to related notes; the graph emerges.

## 4. Optional: link-checker to catch dead `[[links]]`

Since you have lots of `[[links]]` to notes that don't exist, a small script helps keep things tidy:

```bash
# list wikilinks with no matching file
grep -rho '\[\[[^]]*\]\]' *.md draft/*.md | sort -u
```

content.thinking: I need to look into how Telekasten handles tag notation and what the default configuration supports for tagging notes.

content.text:
Telekasten recognizes tags **inside note bodies** (not just YAML). It supports three notations, controlled by the `tag_notation` option (default is `"#tag"`):

## The three tag styles

| Notation | Example | Notes |
|----------|---------|-------|
| `#tag` (default) | `#network #osi-model` | Simplest. **Can't** contain spaces; use `-` or `_`. |
| `:tag:` | `:network: :osi:` | Emacs Org-style, can chain `:a:b:c:` |
| `yaml-bare` | in frontmatter | Structured, cleaner for GitHub |

Whatever you pick, `<leader>zt` (`show_tags`) scans **all** notes and builds a browsable index, and picking a tag lists every note using it.

## Recommended for your GitHub-Wiki setup

Since your notes render on GitHub too, I'd use **`#tag` inline** — it's readable in both nvim and GitHub, and requires no frontmatter. Put tags near the top or bottom of a note:

```markdown
# OSI Model

#network #protocols #fundamentals

## 2. Data Link layer
...
```

Rules for `#tag`:
- No spaces → `#pen-testing`, not `#pen testing`
- They can appear anywhere in the body
- By default Telekasten requires tags to **not** be attached to a word (so a Markdown `# Heading` is *not* treated as a tag — good).

## If you prefer YAML frontmatter

Set `tag_notation = "yaml-bare"` in your config and write:

```markdown
---
title: OSI Model
tags: [network, protocols, fundamentals]
---
```

Let me show where that goes in your config:

content.thinking: I'll offer to add the tag_notation parameter explicitly so they can customize it if needed, even though the default hashtag format should work for most cases.

content.text:
The relevant option would go in that `opts` block:

```lua
opts = {
  home = vim.fn.expand("~/www/wiki"),
  ...
  tag_notation = "#tag", -- or ":tag:" or "yaml-bare"
},
```

`"#tag"` is already the default, so you don't need to add it unless you want to switch.

## Workflow tips

- **Insert a tag fast:** `<leader>zt` (or `:Telekasten show_tags`) lists existing tags — reuse them instead of inventing near-duplicates (`#ai` vs `#AI` vs `#artificial-intelligence`).
- **Keep tags for *cross-cutting themes***, and use `[[links]]` for *direct relationships*. Tags = categories ("all networking notes"); links = the actual graph. In a Zettelkasten, links do the heavy lifting; tags are a secondary index.
- **Be sparing.** 2–5 broad tags per note beats 15 specific ones.
